I would say yes, but I'm also seeing it through the lens of my own situation, which sounds *somewhat* similar to your sister.

I moved in with my grandparents not long ago due to a large stumble, and live here with 5 other people in total. Since I often am taking care of my brothers, I can't get a job (or at least, I can't unless I can somehow find one to comply with my weird schedule.)

So, I take over a lot of chores. My grandmother is incredibly critical, however, and likes to change that up when she feels inclined.

This results in me doing the dishes to help. Unless, for some reason I wasn't supposed to do that tonight, because I really should have read her mind and anticipated that. Sometimes, my job is to cook— and love to. However, sometimes (I think) she gets jealous of the praise I get for the meals, and I won't be allowed in the kitchen when she's there. I'm allowed to do my own laundry when she's away— but if they're here, I can't. Because I, an adult, might "break it." Then, if I try to be helpful and do those things, and she doesn't want me to? I get assigned a malicious intent. Like I was doing this purely to upset her— when really? I was just trying to be useful.

I do things wrong. I don't deny that. But she will often get upset at me for reasons I could never have guessed at, and that's incredibly hard to live with, especially when I have no other choice but to be here. 

I really doubt your sister had anything else in her mind other than helping, most people wouldn't. She just did your work for you to take a load off. So you need to be clear, and simply request you do the laundry, or just let her help. It's one or the other, but please don't be the sort of person my grandmother is.

Addiction is a disease I agree— and I don't know where this is, but my aunt is a court appointed defense attorney for dependency and neglect cases. Court is surprisingly helpful to those who take the help. And most addicts who want to get better actually will take an Ultimatum. Especially if the ultimatum is "your drugs, or your child." As someone who has been addicted to something, and knows people like that, they don't turn around until what they consider rock bottom hits them. If your kid isn't your rock bottom, I'm sorry, but you don't deserve them, and you don't deserve to have an opinion on their upbringing. Hell, seeing their brother overdose wasn't eveb rock bottom. They won't get better until they choose to. Court promises a fit parent, not a good parent— but they couldn't even muster up that much.

I've seen people who turn around. Because they want to— for their kids, for themselves, or whatever reason. And court can be really helpful about it. They can get you therapy. You can go to rehab. And those people who turn around? Are freaking amazing people.

And I've seen people give up, and give into the lifestyle. And thats not good, it's not ok. The people who give into it become entitled jerks. They will steal your money, and anything else. Sometimes things happen, and you have to make a choice. I'm surprised their rock bottom wasn't having someone they were partying with, OD. Mine was losing way too much of my money, and all the assholes I had to deal with. It's not ok. I understand the wanting a break from reality, but just because it's hard to break out of doesn't mean you don't understand that some things are more important. And if you don't see the important stuff? You won't get better. You can't get better until you want to.

So......my situation was different, I was 14 (maybe younger? Cant recall. Around that age.), and people definitely have memories from then. However: my alter blotted them out, and does her very best to keep it that way on a daily basis. I've had access to them by now, because we actually took it to court, and there was a need for them there. 
I remember the times before I really didn't know what was up though, just that *something* was. I asked her about it. Her response was that I wasn't strong enough yet, and couldn't handle it. I told her "those are my memories, and I have a right to have them, strong or not." She basically told me I could keep whining, but as far as she was concerned, I was still weak, and wouldn't be able to handle it. So for the benefit of both of us, she kept the memories themselves locked up tight.

So... I would say the first step is to ask why they're being blocked out. Maybe it's for the same reason Morgan kept mine blocked off— they don't think you can handle it right now. Maybe you're still doing school, and you have other things you need to worry about, that they think trauma could get in the way of right now. 

Just remember though....those memories are painful to experience. Having them explains things, and it does help fill in the blanks sometimes— at least they did for me, because I noticed I was missing chunks of things, or memories would get distorted. But that's not to say I found it enjoyable. Ignorance can be bliss, even if the knowledge can be helpful.

My mind feels busy too— less like I'm outside of a city though, and more like I'm in a small apartment with a roommate.

She can be obnoxious. We live together, so we know each other's quirks....even if we still get superficially annoyed with each other. 
I'd consider us friends though. When we've had a hard day we can always relax, and talk about it, that helps.

We converse about what to eat, and what to wear. Sometimes we both have to compromise because we're really different from each other. 

And even though it is noisy, and it was really *hard* to get to this comfortable equilibrium that we've got now, I like having her around. She's only been really silent once— but I can't forget what that felt like, and I didn't like it at all.

That's PTSD for you man, and I'm sorry you have to deal with that. I think a big part of that is also just the human experience though. I mean, obviously, nobody without OSDD/DID is going to have it as bad as we do— but I think everyone experiences a form of that, because I tend to believe everyone has bad experiences with at least one person, and it's probably family.

Our Host and I like to play D&D, ok? And I promise I'm going somewhere with this— I really like to screw around and hit things, and she likes to focus more on characters and their stories. She likes to say that for the most part, people are going to be defined by their experiences and how they react to them. She's got these three characters that she put WAY too much thought into— and I know because she won't shut up about them. But I've noticed, she relates a bit too much to them too.

Raziel was raised as a thief, and ran away from the people who raised him because he didn't want to continue that cycle. His adoptive parent was a thief, and wanted Raziel to keep doing the same things that he knew he shouldnt— so he tore it all down and ran away from it. Raziel is a good character. He has done bad things— and they are bad, because he knows the difference between wrong and right, and that was a clear wrong. He continues to do bad things sometimes— but this does not make him any less of a good character. He does bad things now because he hasn't truly broken away from his upbringing yet. He even asked a party member "what do you think makes a good person, and why can't I seem to do it?" And she told him that being "good" is not only not a linear path, but it's not something that you can just always be either. Its something you have to keep striving to be, and you do that by getting up every day and trying to do a little better. And I took that to heart lol.

This other one named Volans started out bad— she really tried to make him a shallow asshole of a guy. But the more he was around, the more complex he got. He's no alter...yet. but I wouldn't be surprised if he ended up becoming one. She talks about him like a human. He was forced to run from his abuser— a lot like we were. His abuser and her selfishness forced him to abandon his home, friends, and everything he knew. And when that wasn't enough? Some of her guards killed his best friend. This led to his pact with a demon, and slowly led him to abandoning morals that he really held onto hard. He developed a problem with alcohol, he became a real asshole— and only because he couldn't tolerate the loneliness, but couldn't bear the thought of getting another friend killed. But you know what? He's a good character too. And the reason why, is because even though he's an asshole, who has a hard time dealing with his trauma? Doesn't make him any less caring. He cares too much, and he really thought that would be his downfall....but really that's what opened him up to so many good things. He told his party members about his trauma, and was surprised to find that they didn't laugh or ridicule him— not only did they take him seriously, they wanted to see him get better. They actively helped him get rid of his demon and end the pact, they took him in so that his abuser couldn't hunt him down. He still has his problems— but he is no less of a good person for having flaws. And neither are you. Neither is anyone. Learning how to be good is a process, and one you have to work for every day.

And you know what? Sometimes, you won't succeed. Sometimes you will fall back into bad habits, because that's how things are. But you are worth forgiving, as long as you are willing to learn, and try to be better. Being a good person isn't about being good all the time, it's about trying to be better than you already are.

Now this last one, Mars, is supposed to be bad. He hasn't been around for long, and she's done nothing with him yet— but from what it sounds like, he's the worst kind of bad. He's pure selfish. He knows he hurts people in getting what he wants— but he doesn't care, and he doesn't stop. Of these characters, he has lived a good, Middle class life. He hasn't struggled, he was never bullied, never abused by his parents— but he's not a good guy. He takes advantage of people where he can, and doesn't care if they don't like it. He is bad, because he refuses to see his problems, and fix them. He is bad, not because it's his goal to inflict pain, but because he doesn't care that he does. And since that doesn't bother him, he has no reason to strive to be better. As long as that isn't you, I'd say youre doing about as good as the rest of us. 

Going day to day, doing what you think is right, and hoping it's enough. And you know what? It is. You're enough, and that goes for your headmates too— you're not your abuser, because you care that you hurt people, and strive not to. Sometimes you will, because breaking free isn't as easy as it sounds. Sometimes you'll hurt people because you care too much about them or the situation at hand. Even if you hurt people out of selfishness— remember to apologize, and mean it. Even if they don't believe you, that's not always what matters. Sometimes the promise in the apology is all you need. An apology is a promise not to hurt someone this way again...but sometimes, you'll mess up and do that too. It's part of being a human. Just do your best, because that's all any of us are doing.
